What is a risk?

  • Anything that could negatively impact the organization's ability to achieve its business objectives.
  • A risk is the threat that an event, action, or non-action could adversely affect an organization's ability to achieve its business objectives and execute its strategies successfully.

Risk types

Financial risks

  • Risks affecting the financial processes of the company or that have a negative financial impact to the company (accounting and reporting, tax, capital structure etc.).

Strategic risks

  • Risks affecting achievement of the strategic objectives of the company (governance, strategic planning, major initiatives etc.).
    Operational risks
    • Risks affecting the operations of the company (sales and marketing, supply chain, HR etc.).

Compliance and regulatory risks

  • Risks affecting the company's compliance with regulatory requirements (fraud and ethics, liabilities, data protection & privacy, intellectual property, audit managment, securities etc.). These risks could expose the company to fines and penalties from a regulatory agency due to non-compliance with laws and regulations.

Reputational risks

  • Risk that could expose the company to negative publicity.


External risks

  • Exposures that are the result of environmental conditions that the organization commonly cannot influence, e.g., changes in the economy/markets, changes in competitive environment, regulatory/legislative changes.

Internal risks

  • Exposures that derive from corporate decision-making and the use of internal and external resources, e.g., theft and fraud, duplicate payments, inappropriate purchases.


Why do we consider risks?

  • To identify points where controls are needed.
  • To assist with identifying all the relevant risks and the controls that mitigate them.
  • To help formulate additional questions we need to ask to help identify the appropriate controls

What can an organization do to help mitigate risk?

  • Design and implement a solid system of internal controls.
  • Monitor the performance of controls.
  • Take corrective action when controls are not operating appropriately.

Typical risk assertions that should be considered while understanding how the client is addressing risk and controls

  • Occurrence: the transactions actually took place.
  • Completeness: all transactions that should have been recorded have been recorded.
  • Accuracy: the transactions were recorded at the appropriate amounts.
  • Existence: assets, liabilities and equity balances exist.
  • Rights and obligations: the entity holds or controls the rights to its assets and owes obligations to its liabilities.
  • Valuation and allocation: assets, liabilities and equity balances are included in the financial statements at appropriate amounts and any resulting valuation or allocation adjustments are appropriately recorded.
